# LaunchSense

LaunchSense checks the codebase, not the business. The website is the public read: paste a GitHub URL, get a plain report. A coding tool calls the same public read at the hosted MCP address. You do not clone this repo to use it.

This stage is alpha. Alpha has no login. An auth slot exists and is not enforced.

## Connect

```
https://harmless-chihuahua-667.convex.site/mcp
```

Cursor adds that URL under `mcpServers.launchsense`. Claude Code:

```
claude mcp add launchsense --transport http https://harmless-chihuahua-667.convex.site/mcp
```

The client POSTs one JSON-RPC message. The server returns one JSON answer, or a `text/event-stream` when the client asks for one.

## Tools

`launchsense_scan_public` takes `repoUrl` like `https://github.com/owner/repo`. It reads that public repo on our server. Guest limits of 200 files and about 2MB apply. OSV covers up to 50 packages. deps.dev is not asked. The hosted read shares one hourly budget: 200 scans an hour for the shared hosted bucket, and 600 in total across the hosted lane, then the route pauses. The counter holds no part of your network address.

`launchsense_get_report` takes `scanId` and returns the coverage line and the findings.

Those two names belong to this address. The local server under Surfaces has its own names, and its `launchsense_scan_public_notice` scans nothing: it only points back here.

A partial result is not a pass. This address does not read a repo that exists only on a laptop. A private repo uses Sign in on the website.

## Checks

Fixed checks cover secrets, code shapes, dependency names, license text, and project hygiene, plus duplicate files and large files.

License lines are signals, not legal advice. Unknown stays unknown. A model may quote one next look. That quote is not a finding. The priority table always orders the report. The decision API may reorder inside one severity band. The model does not choose which findings exist. Plain-word rewriting and that reorder are in the product and still evolving. No writing provider is configured in this release, so fixed wording is what ships. A reinforcement learning loop, based on what a later scan shows as fixed or still broken, is the next step. It is not a trained model, and it does not train on the code.

## Surfaces

Three notes on surfaces. The first two are not the hosted address:

- A local stdio MCP server (`mcp/main.go`, wired by `install.sh`) reviews a checkout on that machine. The Go module is `mcp/`, and there is no `go.mod` at the repo root, so it starts with `cd mcp && go run .`. `install.sh` writes that command for Cursor, with `cwd` set to the `mcp` folder. It needs Go on `PATH`; without Go the installer says so and registers no server. It is for a checkout of this repository, not for the public address.
  - It speaks MCP over stdio as newline-delimited JSON: one JSON message per line in, one JSON message per line out, with no length header. `initialize` answers with protocol version 2024-11-05. Refused and error lines go to stderr, so stdout carries protocol only.
  - One message may be up to 4 MiB (4,194,304 bytes, the trailing newline included). A longer line is answered with a JSON-RPC error, nothing runs, and the next message is still answered.
  - Its tools are `launchsense_scan_repo`, which reviews the checkout and takes no arguments, `launchsense_report`, which asks the hosted API for a report by scan id, `launchsense_github`, which reports the local `gh` login, and `launchsense_scan_public_notice`, which scans nothing and only names where the public read lives. A tool name this server does not have is a protocol error, so the hosted name `launchsense_scan_public` called here is refused rather than answered with a scan. A missing, wrong-typed, or undeclared argument is refused rather than ignored.
  - `launchsense_scan_repo` reviews `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT`, which `install.sh` sets to the checkout root, so it reads the checkout and not the `mcp` folder. With `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT` unset it reads the checkout above a `mcp` module folder, and otherwise the folder it was started in. `LAUNCHSENSE_ROOT` must be absolute, and a folder that is not a checkout is named in the answer.
  - A report body over 1 MiB comes back marked partial and is never returned as a whole report. An API call gives up after 8 seconds and the local review after 10 minutes, so a call that hangs ends in an error instead of holding the session open.
  - It reads files locally and does not upload them. Usage counts are off unless you answer yes to one question. `install.sh` asks before it records anything and defaults to no; it keeps the answer, with the wording it agreed to, in `~/.config/launchsense/consent.jsonl`. With a yes it sends rule id counts, the harness name, the version, how long it took, and which order source ran. That share carries no code, paths, titles, or function names. `install.sh --enterprise` and `LAUNCHSENSE_DIAGNOSTICS=off` leave it off. The notice for all of this is at `/privacy` and in `docs/PRIVACY.md`.
- A GitHub App installation-token minter (`convex/github/app.ts`) mints a short-lived installation token. No scan flow calls it yet; the connected GitHub App read is roadmap, not built.
- The hosted usage route (`POST /api/mcp/usage`) writes counts only. It needs a deployment secret header, `x-launchsense-usage-key`. When `USAGE_ROUTE_KEY` is unset, it rejects every caller.

Two tables, `usageMeters` and `connectedInstallations`, are defined in the schema but have no reader yet. No query returns them.

## Analytics

Two tables, and one nightly fold.

- `usageEvents` holds one row per MCP protocol action on the hosted address: `initialize`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`. It is the only table this lane writes per call.
- `dailyMetrics` is the rollup. One row per (day, metric, low-cardinality dims). Every dashboard reads this table and nothing else.
- `rollupDaily` runs at 03:20 UTC and folds yesterday. It replaces the day rather than appending, so a retried cron cannot double count.
- `purgeExpiredUsageEvents` runs at 03:40 UTC and deletes `usageEvents` rows past 30 days, bounded at 500 rows a run and reporting when it hits that bound. Separate from the fold because a Convex mutation cannot call another mutation.
- `scans.surface` is new and optional. Nothing writes it yet, so every metric row currently reads `surface` as `unspecified`. The web and MCP write paths are not wired.

The north star is `repos_with_proven_fix`: distinct repositories where a `findingTransitions` row says `state=fixed` and `cause=code_change` and both endpoint scans reached `status=completed`. A fix counted as `advisory_update` or `analyzer_update` is this product shipping a rule pack, so those are three separate metrics from day one and never folded in.

Two guardrails. `partial_coverage_rate` is partial over all analyzed, split by `truncated`, `tree_truncated`, and `errorKind`. `regression_after_fix_rate` is the share of proven fixes whose `ruleId` came back in the next completed scan of the same repo. Both are lower bounds where the read window runs out, and the code says so.

What is never collected, enforced in code by `convex/analytics/privacy.ts`: file content, paths, findings titles, snippets, raw error text, secrets, IP addresses, model names, prompt text, and the OTel Opt-In attributes `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments`, `gen_ai.tool.call.result`, `gen_ai.prompt.variable.*`, and `mcp.resource.uri`. The argument to a scan tool is a repository URL, which is the reason the Opt-In is refused rather than merely not required. `repoKey` is `HMAC(deployment salt, day + "owner/repo")` or absent; the salt comes from `ANALYTICS_DAY_SALT`, so same-day joins work and nothing joins across days. `clientName` goes through a fixed eight-value allowlist, because `clientInfo.name` is client-declared and storing it raw would let one caller mint a new dimension per request.

Names it will not segment on: a repository. The rollup counts distinct repos while it runs and stores only the count, so a stored day cannot be joined back to a repo. Per-rule and per-severity fix breakdowns are not on `dailyMetrics`: `findingTransitions` holds them, and a per-rule dimension would multiply rows for a few hundred numbers.

## Do not claim

The review does not say the app will sell. It does not edit the repo. It does not certify anything. It does not treat a source-available license as open source.
